Teddy Edwards Oral History (Patricia Willard):
Tell us where you were born and where.
I was born April 26, 1924, 821 South Rose Street, Jackson, Mississippi.
There's a birthday that ...(? )...(?)...

Right. One is incorrect. They corrected it later. That was taken from an album I did on Pacific Jazz, where the guy that did the liner notes had the wrong date, and that one seemed to have got into more print than the rest of them!
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]

Yeah, my father was a trombone player, and he played several other instruments -- he played the trumpet and saxophone, clarinet, violin. He was a very, very talented man, you know. But Jazz-wise as far as playing ad-lib, he wasn't anything to brag about. But as far as reading the music, he was fantastic, because he played on the circus bands and marching bands -- and that was his thing, reading the music, you know. I remember seeing some of the books that he had left at home, very difficult books, like the #3 and #4 Overture books, you know, all the real heavy stuff every place! [LAUGHS] Yeah...
Did he teach you to read music?
No, my father left Jackson before I was born, to pursue his livelihood, you know, as a musician.
T. Edwards - 2

And he had other things that he had done. He was a good carpenter, a good tailor, and later on I found out that he was very good at card games, sociable card games, and pool, checkers. He had a lot of things that he could do very, very well.
And my mother stayed home, because she was an epileptic, and she had to stay close to her home people, so that somebody would know, you know, what to do in case of a seizure or something.
What was your father's name?

His name was Bruce Marcus Edwards. Now, he was born in Mississippi. Also I found out a few years ago, in Edwards, Mississippi...somewhere back in there, it was named for some of my foreparents, way back in there... But I never did have too much history on his side of the family. But a cousin of mine did tell me that Edwards, Mississippi was named for some of our relatives way back.

And he moved to Galveston...not Galveston, Beaumont, Texas. That was his base for a long time. And actually, I was 12 years old the first time I ever saw him. And I was already playing. I was playing in a band then. Yeah...
Her name is Theresa Mildred Edwards. She didn't play an instrument. But she was a very good amateur singer, and she had very great skills with her hands, you know, like
T. Edwards - 3
embroidery, crocheting, and knitting, and quilting, and cooking -- anything like that. She was really superb at it.
Did you ...(?)... ...[INAUDIBLE]...

Yeah, from that particular marriage. But I have a half-sister, Gladys McCrane(?), on my mother's side, and I have a sister and a brother on my father's side. My brother, his name is Burkhard(?) Edwards, and the sister's name is Velma. She lives in Los Angeles. She's the librarian out at San Fernando Valley High.
Yeah, but we lived with our grand...with my grandparents.
Did your father ...(?)... (?)...

Yeah. We lived with was my grandparents, because we had to stay close (?) to somebody(?). Actually, my grandmother was more like my mother than my mother, and we were very, very close. And her name was Malvina Smith Reed. Her father was John Smith. He's as far as I know back from that side of the family -- my great-grandfather, John Smith. And we lived there with them. And she was... She had a lot of things she could do well also.
I read ...(?)... that a grandfather of yours was a musician.
Right, he played...
Your grandfather was a ...(?)...
T. Edwards - 4

That's my grandfather on my mother's side, Henry Carson Reed. And they used to call him Professor, and Fess for short -- so everybody knew him around home as Fess Reed. Actually, he was one of the early upright bass players, string bass players in Jazz bands.
Oh!

Yeah, because of the bands in that period were using the sousaphone for the bass, to play the bass parts. But he had been playing...long before I was born playing the bass violin. So he had to be early in the Jazz thing. In fact, we worked together on several different occasions.
He was playing Jazz.
Yeah, yeah.
(?)Who did he play with(?)?

He played with all the bands around the Mississippi...you know, around that territory. He played with several groups and bands and things around home there. But he was a better known bass player in that territory, the Mississippi territory.
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
Well, all right. I was taught, ha-ha, from, oh, a very early age. Like, my mother and my grandmother, in fact the whole family had designs on me playing saxophone
T. Edwards - 5

-- because my daddy had played saxophone. And he had left a picture on the piano of him playing saxophone. And some other things he left that I'll talk about later on... But they always taught me to idolize my Dad, you know, and they wanted me to be like my Dad, a saxophone player, you know. And even before I started with school, they would sit me next to the saxophone section when they rehearsed at my house... See, the bands used to rehearse at my house, you know, bands my grandfather played with, and different other bands, they would rehearse -- because we had a piano in the living room. They would take me and sit me right next to the saxophones. I was maybe about three or four years old, you know. They brainwashed me real good, but it so happened that it worked out, you know. And I had the great love for it even before I started school; I had the great love for the music. And they exposed to a lot of singing around the neighborhood and around the house.
And two doors away from me was...a sanctified church, they called them at that time; and they had a band -- I used to listen to that band.

There was plenty of music all around. They used to have... There was a lot down the street from me, or across the street, and they used to have medicine shows, and they'd have bands play, and the bands would be out playing to draw
T. Edwards - 6
the people to the medicine show, and... There was always plenty of music around, you know.

Yes, and I'd like to get back to the very beginning of my association with the instrument. There was a saxophone player living at our house, renting a room. You know, in ...(?)... plenty of rooms, and two beds in one room and all that type of thing. And he lived there with us... So my mother approached him about teaching me to play, giving me lessons. And he was very happy to do it. And they came to an agreement where she washed and ironed his clothes to pay for my lesson, 35 cents per lesson, you know. His name was Arthur Horn. And he taught me everything he was able to teach me, and after about six months he told me that I was on my own, because he didn't know anything else to teach me. I was 11 years old at the time.

So I was pretty much on my own, and practicing out of the books; you know, the original saxophone book, the Ben Barekan(?) -- because all the guys were studying out of that. I think a lot of guys nowadays... In fact, I heard John Coltrane play a passage the other day from that book. [LAUGHS] I noticed some little lines in there. You know, a lot of guys lifted those lines out of that book. There are some pretty good lines in the book.
T. Edwards - 7

But anyway, I didn't have an instrument. And my uncle, Philip(?) Reed, he bought an alto saxophone with the intention, you know, of doing big things, and he gave it up after a while -- he didn't stay with it. So my mother made a deal with him to wash and iron his clothes to pay for the saxophone. And he agreed to let me have it, you know. So then I had my own instrument.
It was an alto saxophone, C.G. Conn, ha-ha, alto saxophone.

And I continued practicing... And I entered a contest at the Alamo Theatre, an amateur contest. That was the popular theatre, the Black theatre, the Alamo Theatre. And every Monday night they would have this talent contest. And my first entrance I won the first prize hands-down. You know, a kid playing alto saxophone... At that time, Johnny Hodges had made "Jeep's Blues," and it was popular; and I played "Jeep's Blues," you know...
You were competing against adults.

Oh, both...younger people, everybody... You know, anybody that wanted to enter the contest. And I was a young kid, you know, 11 years old playing like that, you know. And I was playing with pretty good maturity for a kid, you know. And I think I won the first prize about
T. Edwards - 8
three weeks in a row at the theatre! [LAUGHS]
What did you win?

Oh, they'd give you three or four dollars or something like that, you know. And that bought me the name in a hurry around my home, you know. And I have to unveil something that I don't unveil too often, that I had a nickname around home. They called me "Babe Ruth" around there during that time, you know. Then it became "Baby Ruth" and "Baby Ray"... You know, they went through all the babies as I came along, you know.
Did it have anything to do with baseball, or just ...(? )...

I don't know. I was wondering if that had something to do with it, because of the Babe Ruth baseball period. But I don't know. But I know that the tag was on me -- and I wasn't a good baseball player by any stretch of the imagination! [LAUGHS] I don't know how that happened. But anyway...
Maybe you ate the candy bars.
Maybe so. Maybe that was it. And that's how I really got started from the very beginning.
Afterwards ...(? )...(? )...
I just kept on practicing. And so, Duke Holliston... His name was Clarence Holliston, but later on
T. Edwards - 9

he called himself Duke Holliston, because in those days you'd be a Duke, Earl or something for a title, you know... He was a saxophone player, and he played with Doc Palmer's Orchestra. And he lived about three blocks around the corner from me.
[HE SEEMS TO HAVE GOTTEN WELL OFF-MIKE]

So one afternoon, I was sitting in the window practicing. I practiced at the piano all the time, because it was convenient. I could look out the window. Whenever I got ready, every afternoon when I came home from school, I had a little bite to eat and went straight to the horn. And then ...(?)... playing later on.

And he asked me if I'd like to try out for the band, you know. Naturally, I was enthused about that, you know. So we made an appointment. And he brought the alto saxophone books from Doc Palmer's Orchestra home. And ...(?)... we got together out on the front porch, because it was in the summertime, it was nice ...(?)..., and we got together, and we went together going through the parts, and I was reading fairly well, you know. So we worked on it. And finally, he decided he would bring a tenor saxophone player in, and have a (?) section. At that time, there was just about (?) saxophones, you know -- usually two altos and a tenor. The baritone wasn't heard too often, and it was a
T. Edwards - 10
three-man reed section. And he had a very fine tenor saxophone player named Lucious Stokes.

So we got together and rehearsed one afternoon up at H.G. Hennington's(?) house. He played some banjo and guitar, and he played guitar with Doc Palmer's band at the time, and he also played piano when we didn't have a piano player. He's one of the legendary guys to me, Mister H.G. Hennington. And we rehearsed at H.G.'s house. That's the first time I rehearsed with the three-saxophone section. That was another trip, learning to play with the other guys and how to blend. It really got me on the track.
Did they have any strange feelings about working with ...(?)...

No, they really inspired me. They were very happy to see me doing as well as I was doing, and they gave me great encouragement. They all knew my grandfather, you know, and knew my family and everybody -- because we were all mixed into the music scene. My father, they knew him and everybody. So they were glad to see me coming along.

And finally, we had the rehearsal with the full band, Doc Palmer's band. And that was another thrill, to have a chance to rehearse with the whole ...(?)... At that time... I could give you the personnel, I think.
[INAUDIBLE]
T. Edwards - 11

The leader was Doc Palmer on trumpet. We also had Zeke Bradley. And our lead trumpet was Man(?) Henderson. He only played the lead as long as it took Doc to learn it, because as soon as Doc learned it, he played the lead. Doc didn't read, but he had fantastic ears and fantastic power and fantastic sound on his trumpet. He is one of the great trumpet players. It's too bad that he wasn't recorded. He was really one of the greats during the Louis Armstrong era. A powerful trumpet player. And he could play all the lead solos, everything! So that was the trumpet section.
They had the one trombone, Butch Rose(?), the trombone player. Then we had Clarence Holliston playing the lead alto, I played the third alto part, and Lucious Stokes played the tenor.

And in the rhythm section, we had Paul Gayten playing the piano, and Luke Palmer played the sousaphone, and H.G. Hennington playing the tenor guitar and the banjo, and Mark Hannah(?) played the drums -- a very excellent drummer.

Mark Hannah(?). I'd like to talk about him for a bit, because he was a very, very abreast man for that period -- or for any period. In fact, he had his own language he spoke, practically. And he was a very immaculate dresser. And he was reading music back in those days. He was the
T. Edwards - 12

only one in the vicinity who could read the drum parts, you know. He was reading the parts... And he was one of the first ones who learned how to play the hi-hat, as we called the sock cymbal in those days, and before that the foot cymbal. You see, that cymbal used to be down on the floor, about 8 or 10 inches off the floor. When it first became popular, the guys... When I first started playing was just about the time when the sock cymbal came on the scene. And before then, they didn't have that after-beat on the sock cymbal; they'd have to beat on the drum, you know...
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]

I don't know how he learned it. But this man was a very wise man. Very wise. He had a great mind, you know. And I imagine he learned it pretty much himself, you know. But he was far, far ahead of his time -- Mark Hannah(?). A very, very brilliant man.

Of course, the band changed personnel. At different periods, they had different guys come in. It changed. And I'd like to mention a couple of guys who were spectacular. You know, so many people got overlooked during that period, you know.
We had a trombone player who came in. His name was Banti. That's all I ever knew, was Banti. [SPELLS] But a fantastic player. Good lead, just like Doc, but you'd play
T. Edwards - 13
or somebody else would play, and he's got it, just like a continuum, you know.

And there was another trumpet player, ...[INAUDIBLE NAME]... It was the first time I saw a guy playing without the buttons on. He had taken the buttons off the keys, you know. And they called him the Viper. And he was some trumpet player, a very spectacular trumpet player.

So I had the experience of working with these guys with Doc's band. That's what really got me on the road. We'd go out on tours during the summer, and it was a spectacular feat(?) at 12 years old going out on a tour, you know.
You toured(?)?
Yeah, my people let me go out on a tour with them, you know.
What did you play? Dances?

Yeah, we played dance ballrooms, you know -- mostly. Then sometimes I would work in a small group with Doc, and another friend of mine, a saxophone player named Ricky Roseman(?). Ricky also played with Doc's band at different times. And we worked at what they called then Pig-Stands, which later became drive-ins. You know, they used to sell pig...pork sandwiches on a bun. And we would out in the front of the places...out in front. And no salary. Doc would pass the hat around the crowd, and people
T. Edwards - 14

would make requests and tip; tip us for playing the requests. So that's how we made... Because all we'd get was a sandwich. Actually, we'd get a break, and we could get a sandwich. But we made pretty good dough...
He split the tips?
Doc would split the tips with us. And it was quite something.
How much would you make?

Oh, sometimes we would make... It was on Sundays when we played the pig-stands, sometimes Saturday, but usually on Sundays... On the weekends, in the afternoons, we played the pig-stands. And sometimes you could come out with two or three dollars a piece, which was big money in those days.

And I also played at a place across the Pearl(?) River, the famous or ill-famed Pearl River, at a place called Bradley's with Doc Palmer. It was like... It had a filling station out in front, and a grocery store, and then a nightclub in the back. And we played in the nightclub part. And our basic salary was three dollars and fifty cents a week, seven nights -- we were making 50 cents a night actually in salary. And the rest we would make in tips. That was the thing, people tipping. And that was quite an experience. [BARELY AUDIBLE] We'd get all these requests,
T. Edwards - 15

and we'd make up our own tunes; you know, you had to learn from scratch... And it was a little band, and we didn't read any music, so that helped me with my ear things -- learning to hear and make things happen.
There wasn't any problem about ....(?)....
No...
Nobody ever said, 'What's that kid doing here?'
No. In that time they didn't have any child labor laws and all of that. But I was pretty tall for my age. In fact...
Well, you're tall now.

Right. I'm six feet tall, and I was the same height when I was 14 years old. So I looked mature, you know. But I never had any problem. People really admired me for being able to do what I could do at the time. I also realized that in order to play those stock arrangements that they had, I had to learn to deal with the clarinet, and so I saved up my money and bought me a clarinet, and taught myself how to play the clarinet.
You taught yourself.

Yeah, I taught myself to play the clarinet. And also, by listening to the guys talk... I used to be riding on the bus and I'd hear the guys talk. I learned from listening, you know, from watching these people.
T. Edwards - 16

Because there was no teacher. We only had one teacher in our whole school system for the Black kids, and we had eight schools -- one teacher. So I might see him fifteen minutes every other month in a class of sixty or better. So I was strictly on my own.

But I would listen to the guys talk about different things. And I heard them talk about a fellow who came from Milwaukee named Davani(?), a saxophone player, and they were talking about how he had, um, what in those times they called cutting everybody's head, you know, like a saxophone battle or that type of thing -- they called it a cuttin' session during those days. He had come through Jackson and cut everybody playing chord style; you know, running the chords. Most these guys might lay on a few licks, or a guy had a big sound or something, but this guy could move on the instrument. So I heard that, and I said, 'Well, I have to learn something about chords.' So I got some books, and I started reading about ...(?)., checking out the chords.

In the meantime, my father had left an Olerum(?) Harmony Book, which was a standard harmony book -- he left it on the piano. And I started reading this book. That's how I learned about harmony. I studied from this book all on my own, just bringing it down as best I could, you know. And actually, by watching and listening, I could orchestrate
T. Edwards - 17
for that orchestra... You know, by the time I turned fourteen, I could write orchestrations for that ...(?)..., just by, you know, listening to the guys and seeing what they talked about.
And that's the way... Most of my training was that way. I just taught myself.
You started writing then.
Oh yeah. I did... The first one that came out right, where all the notes were right, I was 14 years old.
So you kept writing.

Oh, well, I didn't really pursue it. To this day I don't really pursue it. But I just wanted to know about it, you know. But I had the occasion to write some things later on, and I've been writing a little bit here and a little bit there ever since.

I had another opportunity to play with a very fine band around home. The other band was just more modern than Doc's band. It had more special arrangements, we called it in those days. They had several good writers in there. Don Dunbar, whose real name was Lawrence Jefferson, he taught music at Howard University and he was a very fine writer, but he'd come back home and put a band together. He had very good arrangements. He had a fine guitar player that
T. Edwards - 18
was writing at the time, and maybe his name will come to me... Robert E. Lee, that's his name. Robert E. Lee, a fine, fine guitar player and writer. So they had a lot of arrangements, you know...
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
Oh, during those days guys would change them for stage reasons. You know, they'd change their names around. But that was a very good.
Doc Palmer's band played all stocks?

No, they had some special arrangements. But this band had more writers. They had a lot of writers in it. And it was a little more modern band than Doc's band. So they asked me if I would like to play in the band, and so that was a lovely experience to be able to play that music. And they had a very, very good band. I remember some of the guys... Zeke Bradley, a good trumpet player, played with that band. Another fine trumpet player, J.W. Barnes. A good trombone player, Lawrence Johnson. They had a girl piano player, Micki Gwynn ...(?). And there was a saxophone player, an alto player named Bolden(?) Townsend. And Simon(?) Jefferson, a guy with a great big tone on the tenor saxophone; he had a great big tone on the tenor saxophone, a la Chu Berry. And we had...Billy Jones played the drums, and Doug(?)/Dump(?)/Doc(?) Harvey played the
T. Edwards - 19

bass.
That was a very good band, the first band where we really had real sharp uniforms and everything that I played with. You know, that was a (?)really big deal(?).
You were how old when you played with them?

I was 14 when I joined that band. And then Paul Gayten put another little group together called Paul Gayten and His Sizzling Six. We had two saxophones. There was Duke Holliston, and Duke was playing tenor with this group. And we had a guitar player, a fine guitar player, who made some marks later on down in Detroit, named Emmett Slade. And we had Paul on piano and Mark Hannah(?) on the drums. And if I remember correctly, there was a boy named Leon Spann who had come up from Piney Woods, Mississippi, with a band down there; e had worked with the Don Dunbar band; he replaced Doug(?)/Dump(?)/Doc(?) Harvey. And he later ...(?)...(?)... played with the Freddie Johnston Orchestra.
So we had this little thing. We would play matinees every Monday at the ballrooms... The Crystal Palace was the first one that we played. Our first gig was at the Crystal Palace Ballroom...
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
T. Edwards - 20

Yeah. It was on North Farris Street in Jackson. That was the big dance hall where all the bands played. I had an opportunity to hear a lot of great bands, like Earl Hines, Tiny Bradshaw, (?), they had Joe Robicheaux -- a lot of different bands that came through there. I heard Andy Kirk's band, and also Erskine Hawkins. And we also had another ballroom called the Savoy Ballroom, and I used to play there on some matinees that they would have at the Savoy with Paul Gayten's little group. And we also used to broadcast on radio station WJDX in Jackson, which was a big deal. You know, every Saturday we'd broadcast...! [LAUGHS] And we were pretty hot stuff around at that time...
When were you doing this?
Round about 1938. Yeah, around 1938, '39, like that. I was getting a good start, a good start.
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]

I don't know if they had any type of recording equipment around Jackson during that time. Because during that period, everybody had to go to Chicago to record. I remember the legendary Little Brother Montgomery used to play house parties at my house, and my grandfather played with him... He was Paul Gayten's uncle. And Little Brother...they used to have to go to Chicago to
T. Edwards - 21

record. And there was another fellow that my grandfather... Mister Walters. He used to go to Chicago, my grandfather and him, to make records. I think he's the guy that really made the first recording on the "How Long Blues"(?)/ "Howlin' Blues"(?) -- a guy named (?)Mister Walters(?)... Q: What was his name?
Mister Walters. I can't remember his first name. But he played the steel bodied guitar. You know, in those days, the blues players would sing the blues, and they...
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]
...used to go to Chicago to make records. But there was no recording equipment in Jackson, down that far during that period. Q: [INAUDIBLE QUESTION]

Oh, a band that really impressed me, and nobody never, ever mentions this band... A band that came from Little Rock, Arkansas -- Gay(?) Floyd. They had a fantastic band. They had a five-man reed section. They had the two tenors, alto and the baritone. They had full brass, a full band. They had a sleeper bus; you know, the first sleeper I saw, where you could sleep in the bus, you know. And they had a whole slew of writers. Practically most of the horn players could write. The one I really remember is
T. Edwards - 22

R.O.C. Hampton, Riley Hampton, who did a lot of string work for Chess Records through the years; you know, a lot of Chess big hits. He did the writing for them, you know. But that's one of the first bands I heard where they really were voicing the music really big; you know, they had that big sound. And I used to hear them play...

They had a...oh, a great player... The piano player was fantastic. They used to call him "Screw-Loose"; he was kind of strange, you know. But he could play, and he was fooling with way-out harmonies back in those days, you know. He was somewhere else with the harmonies on this piano, you know.

In those days, the big bands had an entertainer... In fact, Doc Palmer's band had an entertainer who sang and directed the band. His name was Alex McKinney, and he used to try to imitate Cab Calloway -- we used to call him Cab. But he'd sing... We didn't have a microphone; you know, he'd sing through the megaphone during those days.

But getting back to the other band... They had a guy who was an entertainer. This man was so spectacular, named Cleophus Jackson. The Gay(?) Floyd Orchestra... This guy was spectacular. He knew all the arrangements, everything. And the movements that he made were classic, before this... He was a whole production himself, you know.
His dances(?)?
T. Edwards - 23

Yeah, just movements with his body and how he kept the tempo going, and he knew where all the licks was, the little things -- and it was very clever. You know, he wasn't really dancing, but he had these movements that he would keep going, you know. And he was really conducting this band; really conducting this band. He knew every part of every arrangements, and everything... And he did it where it looked beautiful, with finesse, you know. He was classy. Too bad he wasn't put on film in front of this band at some time, you know, during his career.

The only thing I ever heard of him was down through Louisiana, Mississippi, down through Arkansas -- down through that way, you know. But they really had some band. Yeah. And I heard, oh, so many bands that came through.

Now, Jimmie Lunceford I wanted to hear. But Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington, the whole time I was at home and could go and hear bands, they never played for the Black dances. Maybe they couldn't afford them or something...
They came through?
They came through, yeah, but they would play for White dances, you know. During those days it was highly segregated. Like, if it was a band that the White people
T. Edwards - 24
wanted to hear, they would have a little section of seats roped off for them, where they could come to the Black dances and hear the music anyway.
[INAUDIBLE]

Oh yeah. But they had a section, a special section for them, where they had these bench-like seats, you know, almost like a stadium type seat -- and they would sit in that section and hear the band. You know, they couldn't come down and dance, but they could sit up there and hear the band.

So when Duke Ellington came to town, I... I was determined to hear Johnny Hodges. So they were playing a dance down at the White armory, they was playing...at the White auditorium downtown. I was about fourteen. So I went down there. And they had this big guy, you know, like the security guy by the front, by the door, you know... So I went up to him and I told him...I said that I was studying music, and Johnny Hodges, my idol, was playing with the Duke Ellington band, and I really wanted to hear him, you know. And he thought it over. [LAUGHS] He stood there and he thought it over. But, uh... He knew I really wanted to hear the band, you know, and so... He took a chance on is job, really. So he opened the door and he pulled me over to the door, and he says, "Now, look. Do you see those steps up
T. Edwards - 25

there?" -- [the steps by the bandstand.] He said, "Do you see those steps up there? You go up there and sit on those steps, and don't you move!" [LAUGHS HEARTILY] I said, "Okay," you know, and that's what I did. And every now and then, he would check up to see if I was still sitting on those steps. And that's where I first heard Johnny Hodges and the Duke Ellington Orchestra. I didn't get a chance to say anything to any of them or anything, but I sat there on those steps and heard that band. And after it was all over, I left and I thanked him, you know, and went home. But I was determined to hear Johnny Hodges play, you know.
[INAUDIBLE]
Oh, I was just thrilled to death to hear that band, to hear Johnny play, you know. Yeah, it was really-really-really something special to me.

Oh, during the summertime we would make tours, like, through parts of Alabama, Louisiana, and East Texas, and different places in Mississippi... In fact, I've got a thing that I wrote called "Hard Times In '29" that I'm going to get somebody to record one of these days, you know... But I remember all of these things that went down.

But getting back to the kids... It was really very strange. Right down the street, a White fellow had a store named Mister Mack. And his kids were beautiful, you know. And he taught respect for everybody in the neighborhood. No problems, you know. But there were just certain places you'd go, you'd run into it, and there you go -- you got to deal with it. You know, you'd have to deal with it.
You never knew exactly where.

Yeah... But you had a pretty good idea. As long as you stayed in a certain range, you were doing pretty good. But if you got out of that territory, then you'd have to deal with it, you know. And I could never really generate any hatred for those kids, because I could kind of understand where they were coming from. They were taught this hatred, you know. They were taught this. And it was a sickness. I could see this. Even when I was a kid, I could see that it was a sickness. So I would deal with it the best way I could. If I had to fight, I'd fight. And run? I'd rather run first! You know?
[INAUDIBLE]

Yeah, but you had to deal with it, you know. And you'd go down sometimes, you'd be down in town, and one of them would walk over to you and hit you, because he knew you couldn't do anything about it -- because the policeman on the corner was not going to defend you. You know? You'd just have to take it and keep walking, you know. Maybe one day you'd catch him out somewhere! But these are the things that used to go on, you know...
How did the other states ...(?). ... compare with Jackson?
With Mississippi?
Yes.

Most of those southern states were really tough. I really think... Louisiana could be very cold during those days, could be very-very cold. And in fact, I remember when we used to play up on Texas Avenue in Shreveport, Louisiana, when the dance let out at two o'clock, at 2:15 the streets had better be clean, because the cops would come through ten or twelve deep and rip every head available with a nightstick -- you know, just out swinging a nightstick. You had to have the street clean, you know.
And there was a lot of places in the South where, [STUTTERS] when the-when the-when the-when the-when the
T. Edwards - 52

police that was policing the dance, one man, when he gets ready to go home, he'd blow the whistle. That's the end of the dance. You stop right then, where we are in the song. Don't finish. If he decides he's ready to go home, he'd blow the whistle and that's it! The dance is over.

[HEARTY LAUGH] I remember they used to pull that! You know, when he got to us, he said, 'This is it.' He'd blow the whistle. No special time. Whenever he felt like it. That was it. The dance was over.

And a lot of strange things go on down through that South, you know. [HEARTY LAUGH] Yes, Man-wise and Nature-wise, you know. Mosquitos be comin' at you on the bandstand... I remember down in Lake Charles, Louisiana, we used to...Lafayette, Lake Charles, down that way, we used to burn rags on the bandstand on a bucket to keep the mosquitos away, you know -- and the mosquitos would come right on through that smoke and hit you anyway! [LAUGHS] Sleep under nets, you know. It was pretty wild.

But the people, they just... It's a strange, strange love goes on in that South, you know. A strange love. For instance, like, at the big chain stores that I was talking about earlier...I was talking about Piggly-Wiggly, A&P and those stores... Now, you would go and help those guys
T. Edwards - 53

unload, like when they had to get the new vegetables and canned goods. We could go in and help them, stack them up on the shelf and clean the vestibules, and put all of this stuff up, unload it and everything. And they'd be just as nice to you, you know, and while you're doing it... Because they'd usually give you some of it, you know, and you'd have something to take home.

But when you finished, they said, 'Okay, it's time to go.' And right away, that means it's time for you to get out of there in a hurry, because they're gonna start throwing everything at you! [LAUGHS] So we'd get so we just... They'd be throwing oranges and apples at us, and we'd just stand up there and catch 'em, and get us a box and put 'em off to the... You know, catch 'em and put 'em off to the side. The more they'd throw, the more we'd catch, and the first thing we've got is a big box and then split. But they'd turn on us just like that, you know! And you'd been helping them! You'd go back next week and do the same thing! They'd be nice while you helped them do all the work! It was pretty wild, you know.

And we used to have to go through the neighborhoods delivering clothes. Like, my mother and most of the families used to wash and iron the White people's clothes, so you'd have to deliver them in the morning and in the
T. Edwards - 54

afternoon, and you'd have to deal with these kids, you know. They would gang you, you know. And they had a very chicken method of doing it sometimes. Sometimes they'd send a kid maybe four or five years old, and they'd start kickin' you, kickin' you -- and then they'd want to know why are you bothering that kid. See? Just to ease their conscience or something, I imagine.
But there was a lot of good people in the South, and a lot of the other kind, you know. But you just have to learn how to deal with whatever the situation was.

Back to Louisiana again, over in Shreveport, Louisiana. I remember I was over there with the Don Dunbar Orchestra. And some kids in the neighborhood were studying music, and they heard about this young kid playing, so they came over, and we fooled around, blowing the horns, one evening I imagine at about 9:30. And we were living in this big rooming house, 450 Oakland Avenue -- I'll never forget it. And there was a White family that lived next door. And evidently, they called the police and said we were disturbing the peace or something. And I'm upstairs with the kids, and the rest of... A lot of the guys in the band were downstairs, playing cards with some of the ladies that lived there, you know. And the police just came in, didn't ask any questions -- and they just started whuppin' heads.
T. Edwards - 55
You know, just whuppin' the guys in the band, and the girls -- everybody. Just started swingin' their billy-clubs.

That's the kind of stuff they used to do down there! It could get pretty wild, with that racial thing down there during those days. They tell me it's much, much better now in general -- in general, you know. Even in Jackson, my people tell me... In fact, my Aunt's husband owned The Jackson Advocate, the Black newspaper there before he passed, and she runs it now... But he used to try to get me to come back home. I'll go there when I can get around to it. But he used to tell me, "Come back, because people want to see you, people want to know you." And then he said, "You'd be surprised. There are White people that know about you that want to meet you and want to see you," you know. So evidently, they are making some different changes down there now, you know.

Getting back to the music, I'd like to mention a young man that I'm very proud of. He's Vice President of the college in Meridian, Mississippi. And he had the college band there when he was the band-master. And two years ago he brought his school band to the Junior Rose Bowl out here in Los Angeles, and he came by to see me. It was really nice to see that he had done so well. I started him out
T. Edwards - 56

when I was fourteen years old, teaching him to play the saxophone. We were the same age. We were in the same class in school. And I started him out. He ended up really being something. And he has two kids who they tell me are really spectacular musicians. So it looks like we started something!
His name was Carl Lee Otis. And as most of the band-leaders did, when they became bandleaders, he had to get a title -- so he's Duke Otis! [LAUGHS]

And his brother... He was telling me something really funny about his brother. His brother was named John, and I was teaching John to play the clarinet. And he was doing pretty good. And the notes had the alphabets over them in the book, you know... And one day he came upon a page that didn't have the alphabet, and he couldn't play a thing! He had been reading the alphabets instead of the notes! [LAUGHS] Yeah, it was pretty neat.
Also during that time...
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]

I don't know the name of the college. It's a ....(?). .... college. But it's the only Black college in Meridian, or they only have one... They used to have two in Jackson. There was Cameron College and Jackson College. But when the state took over Jackson and made it Jackson
T. Edwards - 57
State, then they bought up the Cameron College properties which were down the street a little ways and across the street, and made it all a part of Jackson State.

Now, Jackson State College was located on Lynch Street, the same street that my first school was located on -- and it was called Jim Hill. We went from the First Grade through the Ninth Grade at Jim Hill. And some time later, I found out that Jim Hill had been the Secretary of the State of Mississippi during the Reconstruction period. And also, I found out after I got to California that John R. Lynch was the man that Lynch Street was named after, and he was also a Congressman, a Black Congressman during the Reconstruction period.

And I had some great teachers, very wonderful people. And later on, after I finished the Ninth Grade, I went to Lanier High School. And they were just beginning to get a school band together. Before then, Professor Harley had taught music in eight schools, so we would see him about fifteen minutes every month, or maybe every other month. So we decided to extend the music program. And Professor Mosely came up from Louisiana, Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He had been teaching at Southern, and he began teaching there. Before then, they only had a choir, of which Miss M.D. Mannen(?) was the choir director.
T. Edwards - 58
By the time he got there, I was pretty well advanced, and I was helping him teach the saxophone players and the clarinet players, getting them started in the early stages there.

I had a lot of good moments at (?) high school. From there I played in several band contests throughout the state, and I either won first or second prize on clarinet or saxophones. I ended up always going away with two trophies. That is, until they disqualified me because I was working with the bands around home. They declared me a professional, and so that was the end of my amateur career!
Q: [INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
Yeah, I was still in high school. But I was actually out making money. So they disqualified me. But my trophies and everything are still there.

In fact, I left school in the Eleventh Grade. My Uncle, (?) Bernard(?) Reed and his wife, who was like my second mother, Lydia, they moved to Detroit. And as soon as he got himself going pretty well, anybody from home who wanted to come to Detroit, who figured they had a better chance...and he was sending for them. So he sent for me, and I went there, and I worked in his grocery store, and I started finding my way around.
T. Edwards - 59

It was during the summer when I went there, in 1940. And I started going down to the Bandbox, which was the musicians' club, where musicians would come in and hang out. And they had a piano there, and the guys would sit around and jam until the phone rang, then one of those leaders would go answer the phone, and he'd come and say, 'Well, I need a trumpet, I need a saxophone, I need a drummer, blah-blah-blah-blah' -- that's now you got gigs. So I was giggin'...got gigs that way around Detroit on the weekends.

And I met a lot of people there, especially one guy, a very fine friend of mine... At that time he was called Big Bill Moore; now they call him Wild Bill Moore. A saxophonist. I imagine you're familiar with him. And I'll talk about him later on in our California period, you know. But I was sixteen years old, you know, and I was a pretty fly little guy, you know. And the older guys, they would really put you through the test. During that time, "Liza" and "Tea For Two" and "Body and Soul," those were the tough numbers that they would play, you know. And we would play, and they would take me through all the keys with them and everything. But I was staying pretty sharp, because I was practicing hard, and really, really working on my instrument.
T. Edwards - 60

And a friend of mine...well, one of the guys from home who had played Don Dunbar's orchestra, Simon(?) Jefferson, he invited me to play...to come down and play with him on his gig at a place on St. Antoine, just below Adams in Detroit, called the Turf Bar. And they had one of those bandstands behind the bar, high bandstands, you know. So I used to go down and sit in with him. So eventually, I started making myself a little name around the city. So I started getting calls on different kinds of gigs and things.

I remember one gig I played that was kind of interesting. I played out on Eight-Mile Road at Jack Johnson's, the ex-heavyweight champion's place, and he was like the host. And we had a very fine group there. I was working with a drummer named Johnny Johnston, and the piano player who played with him was an excellent pianist Johnny Van(?). Johnny Van was quite a guy. He had been deeply in love with this young lady who had passed, and he carried her pictures in his briefcase all the time, and when he would come to the job he would sit her pictures on the piano and play to her. And you never heard such soulful playing as this guy sitting there playing to this girl. It was kind of sad. But what he got out of it was something. It was really spectacular.
T. Edwards - 61

But anyway, getting back to the music. Down in Paradise Alley, that's where the action was. The Turf Club was there on St. Antoine. They had the D&C across the street, where we used to go over there and jam. And they had some very well-known saxophone players who used to play around there. A guy named Moon Mullins and his partner Lamont, and Larry DeVito, a very fine Italian tenor saxophone player, who was really a great player.

In fact, this place is where I first met Yusef Lateef. Now, his name was Bill Evans at the time. In fact, I taught him... I was the first guy to teach him the chord changes to a song. It was "Coquette", "My Little Coquette." Yeah...

And there were so many great players around there. And on Hastings Street, they... That was about a block over from St. Antoine. Adams was the main vein, going east and west. They had the big Plantation...

...Club on Adams Boulevard, which I worked later when it became the Plantation -- I will talk about that after a while.

And then the other main vein, where the action was, where all the prostitutes and pimps hung out, was Hastings Street. All the way up and down Hastings, there was guys in the daytime, they'd be running their three card molly, and
T. Edwards - 62
(?)ing the greasy pig with the shells and the pea, and all kinds of games would be going on. And they had bars all up and down that street.

My first job up on Hastings Street was at a place called the Ace Bar, and I was working with the legendary band-leader from George E. Lee. And he was an elderly man, and he was singing and using a megaphone, you know -- that was quite an experience.

And I used to go all up and down the street to different places and play. They had a place called the Cozy Corner, where Bill... Wild Bill Moore had the band up there. And Milt Jackson was just beginning to get himself together during that period, and he used to be running all over town to different places, jamming. His brother would pack one end of the vibes and he'd have the other end -- and his brother also played bass. And they would be all the place, playing the different scenes.

And also on Hastings Street was a bar called the Champion Bar. That's where I first met Gene Ammons. He came over from Chicago with the King Kolax band -- a trumpet player. And Kolax was from Jackson also, but he left before I came on the scene. Now he's President... He's a union delegate in Chicago. Anyway, I met Ammons and them, and I used to go over there and play with them. I was still
T. Edwards - 63
playing my alto at the time, and I used to go and sit in with them. And we had a great rapport. I had a lot of great times over there.

The next, though, was a guy named Effie(?) playing tenor in this real dive. And he had a great sound, playing the saxophone. All he did was play the blues mostly, but he really had a great sound. I can't remember his last name.

And there was another little bar there where one of the big-name pimps, whose name was Fortree(?) at the time... I can remember once when one of his friends passed, they had a Cadillac funeral. They had 26 Cadillacs. You know, when one of the pimps died, they'd have a Cadillac funeral, a Lincoln Continental funeral. They'd really do it up, you know! [LAUGHS] You couldn't be in the funeral unless you had one of those cars.

And those guys, they used to really live it up. Like, nightclub owners used to do things that they don't do now. They'd go and patronize each other. The guy would come in and he'd set up the whole bar. Which is nothing but promotion! -- you know. And they really-really-really lived it up.
And later on, they built a club called the Three Sixes on East Adams. That's where I first saw the legendary T-Bone Walker doing his trip down there. And he was something
T. Edwards - 64

special. Actually, T-Bone opened up the guitar players. All the guitar players out today playing guitar owe T-Bone a debt of gratitude, because he really helped them. Do you remember the thing he made with Freddie Slack? I can't remember the name of the song. Anyway, he played a classic solo, and every guitar player since then has played some parts of that solo.

But anyway, I had played...began to get known, and I first met Sonny Stitt when he came to Detroit with the Trenier twins. The Trenier twins had a big band. They were from Alabama State, and they were out on the road. That's where I first met them, was in Detroit. They also had in the band with them... They had Joe Morris, a trumpet player who had a band and some big records later, and a very fine tenor saxophone player, Don Hill...
Don Hill ...(?)...
He's still with them. But he was playing alto at the time. Right.

And they had an excellent tenor player named Morris Lane, a great saxophone player, Morris Lane, which he... I had first met Morris earlier when he came over from Gary, Indiana, with a saxophone player who had a band... His last name was Perry. I can't remember his first name, but the last name was Perry. He's living around Bakersfield,
T. Edwards - 65

California now. And he really had a beautiful sound on the tenor saxophone. Who else was in the band...? They had Eugene Gilbo(?), a fine pianist and arranger that worked with the Treniers for years and years.
He always played standing up.

Right, he played standing up. But he was sitting down in those days. He didn't start standing up until he got the small group together, when they disbanded the band. They disbanded the band to go with Jimmie Lunceford's band, the twins did. They went with Jimmie Lunceford and they disbanded that band.
I met them in Detroit. This must have been around about 1941 when I first met them. And they had a very fine band. A really good band.

During this period I met the great saxophonist, Lucky Thompson. He was just coming out of high school. And I had entered school. I had entered Northern for a while. But my grandmother always had me going back and forth between Detroit and Jackson. Because when she got ready to come to Detroit, she didn't care whether I was going to school or not. I'd have to drive back to Jackson and ride back up with her, and ride back up with her, and take her back, and then come back to Detroit! So I began to lose out in school a little bit...
T. Edwards - 66

Yeah, there were so many great players around Detroit during that time. They had an excellent pianist named Willie Anderson. He was terrific. And I also met Rudy Rutherford, who was a fine clarinetist, around that time. He was from Detroit. And we were like the young alto players around there -- Bernie Peacock, Sonny Stitt, Rudy Rutherford. And then Wardell came to town, Wardell Gray, when he came to town playing alto he was added to the list. So we had a lot of young saxophone players on the scene.
My gigs were picking up more and more, as I got better known around the city.

I'll never forget December the seventh, the night that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor. I was working at a place called Enrico's over on Rivard(?) and Watson. And people came running in the place, shouting 'We're at war! We're at war! We're at war!' I never thought of anything like that, you know. And we had a nice band in there, playing for the floor show. We had an all female impersonator floor show.

I was really getting plenty of experiences in Detroit, you know... [HEARTY LAUGH] I even played some taxi dances, and I did some nightclub work out in Dearborn, where they had a chorus line and everything -- I don't remember the name of the place. And I was just adding to the
T. Edwards - 67
experiences. And I'd still go by the Bandbox and play with the guys, you know, because that kept you sharp and kept your name alive, and you'd start growing.

Then as my work progressed, the guys said, "Well, man, you're going to have to join the union," you know -- because I started working better jobs where you had to belong to the union. So that's when I first joined the union, in 1941. They had an ex-saxophone player who was the Black representative in the union, named Lanky(?) Bowman, and he really controlled that whole area, you know... [LAUGHS] But he was a great guy.
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
No, they only had one local in Detroit. But we had one Black representative to handle all the Black musicians! [LAUGHS] Yes...
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
In '41 I should have been 17. Yeah, at 17 I joined the union. So that put me, you know, into a little better class as far as for getting different kinds of jobs.

Yeah, I was still going to the Bandbox to latch on to different gigs. And I had the pleasure of hearing guys like Lester Kerr, who was a trumpet player, and his brother Gloster Kerr, and the great Cecil Lee, a trumpet player, and Russell Smith -- among some of the really great guys that I
T. Edwards - 68
heard playing during that period. Oh, he was a fine player. A fine player.

And I worked at a place on Grand River with Johnny Johnson, the drummer, again... And we had a three-piece group: Johnny Johnson, Hank Jones playing piano, and me playing the alto saxophone. And later on, Hank and I, with a guitar player named Al Smith, we organized a little trio. We had it going, had a job booked out in Idaho or someplace, some people were going to send us to Idaho or something...! So my grandmother wanted to come to Detroit again! [LAUGHS] So I had to go back to Jackson and take her back to Detroit again. She wanted to see the family, and my uncle...

But he was... My uncle, I must say again, he was very beautiful to me, and his wife, Lydia, was very beautiful. They had a daughter named Greta. The whole time I stayed with them, they never charged me a penny for anything. And I was out working and making money. They wouldn't let me spend anything, you know. They were so great to me -- and anybody else from the family who wanted to take a shot at Detroit. We had really great times together.

So I brought my grandmother back. And I came back, and things had changed around a little bit. I started working with a bass player out of Columbus, Ohio, named Tweed(?) Beard. And we had a very good group going.
T. Edwards - 69

Before I get any further, there's one guy I want to mention. Because this guy was so spectacular, I don't think I've ever heard anybody play a saxophone more personable than he did. He sounded like he was inside of his instrument. I rehearsed with him a few times at a club called The Twelve Horsemen, over on Jonorra(?) Street. And this guy had the warmest feeling! You could just feel it, you know, like there was heat coming off his instrument when he played. His name was Eddie Loven(?). And some years later, he went with Andy Kirk's orchestra. He died at 24 from tuberculosis. And Howard McGhee told me that Eddie Loven, at that time, when he died, he was as good as anybody playing a tenor saxophone, if he wasn't the best. And he never made a record! -- which is really kind of sad. You know, the guy never made a record. So I have to mention Eddie Loven(?), because he was really something special.
Did he come from Detroit?
Yeah, he was a native of Detroit.
And that was the only place you heard him.
Yeah. The only place I heard of him playing, you know. Also Julius Watkins, the French horn player, he came up around that same period.
Detroit has turned out so many excellent musicians, you know, because they had a great music system in the school
T. Edwards - 70

system. In fact, Cass Tech there in Detroit, if you came out of there you were considered equivalent to a two-year-college...a junior college education in your specialty, because you could really specialize in whatever you were doing. I passed the aptitude test there. I went there later for a while. But I'll explain later why I left. I had to give it up, you know.
Your grandmother ...(?)...
No, not her this time! It wasn't her. It was me this time. But I'll get around to that. But it was really, really great times in Detroit during that period.

Joe Louis had been drafted in... He used to train at the Brewster Center down from where I lived. I used to live on Erskine and Bovian(?), and the Brewster Center was on Hastings one block below Erskine. So it was only one big street, about a block-and-a-half away. That's where Sugar Ray came up, over there in the boxing thing... You know, he had... When he first went in the Army, I used to see him sitting on the steps at the Norwood Hotel down on the (?). He'd sit out on the steps, and he had on his G.I. uniform and everything... Oh, he was really a beautiful man, you know, his complexion and everything. I would just look at him, and he used to just glow, you know. And I remember Sugar Ray used to come down to the Paradise Bowling Alley
T. Edwards - 71
before he'd have a fight going, and the guys (?)he'd be with(?) would be betting everybody on the fight. They had all kinds of money.

Detroit was really a sporting town, you know. Everything was going. All kind of hustles were going on. Whatever your game was, it was working, you know. And the numbers were very, very big then, you know, where you put so much on a number and then the number comes out that day, and if you catch it, you win. And there were good odds, 500-to-1. And the numbers man had a lot of money, and they'd be sportin' it up, or just livin' it up... It was really good times. Even though times were a little hard, it was still great times.

In fact, they still had WPA bands around during that period. WPA bands were bands that the government had sponsored, when President Roosevelt was bringing the nation out of the Depression. And WPA bands were...
[INAUDIBLE COMMENT]

Right, right. The WPA bands were up until around '40, 41, during that... Around that period the WPA bands were still existing. And that was a band where the guys would get paid to rehearse, and then they would play maybe once a week in the park or something, just to keep people employed -- because times were still hard then, you
T. Edwards - 72
know. I used to go down into the project and listen to Fergie... Mr. Ferguson had the band in the project where I used to live, and I used to go down and listen to them rehearse, the WPA bands.

And they had all kinds of music going on around there. There was another place that had (?) music called Little Sam's, down in Black Bottom, way over into the ghetto. I used to work down in there, you know! [LAUGHS] I did some getting-around, all right.

And I still kept my ears tuned to the radio quite a bit, and listened to the records on the jukebox, and I had my choice of people I liked, and I went ahead with people that, you know, I was impressed by.

I'll never forget one guy that I was really impressed by. He was out of the Johnny Hodges mode. And I never hear anybody talk about this guy, but he was a great saxophone player. I hate to put emphasis on what color, but he was a White saxophone player -- and there hadn't been many of them broken the mold from the Wayne King type of thing with the heavy vibrato and all that. And he was a beautiful saxophone player, Johnny Bothwell. He had a band for a while.
And there was another guy named Hal McIntyre. I used to love the way he played lead alto with his band. And he
T. Edwards - 73
had a very fine tenor saxophone player with him named Dave Matthews I used to listen to. Yes, those were really great, great artists.

Yeah, and they had some local boys who were really great players. Sam Donohue, who had a band some years ago, a tenor saxophone player. And Bobby Burns, a trombone player who was a bandleader. His father taught at Cass Tech. In fact, he was the head of the Music Department, his father, over at...
[INAUDIBLE QUESTION]
Oh, I'll get to that in a few minutes. Okay? [LAUGHS]

There was plenty of good listening around the city during that period. I remember going down to the Michigan Theatre. That's where I first heard Frank Sinatra with the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra. That was a real treat. And Timmy Rogers was on the bill, the comedian and musician; he was on the bill. That was an exciting show.

They also had a theatre, the Paradise Theatre, where all the name Black bands would play -- Ellington, Lunceford, Andy Kirk. A lot of different acts. Cab Calloway. I first saw Count Basie in the Paradise. And I first saw Earl Fatha Hines when he came to Detroit, and I heard Billy Eckstine with him at the time, and also Sarah Vaughan, Charlie Parker
T. Edwards - 74
Dizzy Gillespie -- that hand. Hell, that was a real monster he had there, that particular band.

I also saw over there people like Butterbeans and Susie. Ha-ha, that takes you back, huh? They had ...(?)..., and they had Honi Coles, the great tap dancers there. And Elaine(?) Dixon and [INAUDIBLE NAME]. The great Baby Lawrence, who was probably the greatest tap dancer who ever lived. It's a shame that they didn't get him on film the way that some.... They didn't leave enough of him on film. Because he was... To me he was like the Charlie Parker of dance. I remember I used to see him on Adams and St. Antoine. He'd stand up by the mailbox and dance two or three hours, and set up a whole show, just him and the mailbox on the corner. Just spectacular creativity that could come out of that man.

Pete Nugent, a classy dancer. And Kilroy... He was a dancer, a tap dancer. Oh, they had the Groundhog, and Leon Collins. There were so many great performers. Patterson and Jackson, a comedy team; I know you've heard of them. And Bunny Briggs; I first saw Bunny Briggs there. I saw Bill Robinson dance there at the Paradise Theatre.
