this guy wasn't even a Jazz fan or anything -- he met Charlie Parker and he moved Charlie Parker into his house that night. That's when he was married to Doris. He moved him into his house that night...heh-heh...! So we went by and got him, and hung out with him.

And I'll never forget. We were back near the bathroom, talking, and he was saying how he really regretted pawning the saxophone that he had with the Eckstine band when they were playing at the Club Riviera in St. Louis. He said he got his best sound on that horn. He really regretted losing that instrument.

Anyway, everybody was planning for the big night at Jack's Basket Room after-hours. And Leroy had fixed him a big steak and everything, and he was already feelin' good -- he had fresh clothes and everything, heh-heh. And when we got to Jack's Basket Room, the place was loaded. Everybody was waiting on Charlie Parker. In the audience that night I remember was Preston Foster...no, Robert Preston, that's the one, and Ava Gardner and Turon(?) Bey(?), and all kind of musicians and celebrities. Stan Kenton's band was in town that night, and all the guys were there.
This first set that he played on was with Jimmy Bunn on piano; Jo Jones, Daddy Jo The Drummer, on drums; and Curtis Counce I think was playing the bass; and June Christy
T. Edwards - 151

singing on the set -- just the five of them. They did the first set, Charlie Parker and June Christy on the front line. And it was really beautiful, you know. That's when I fell in love with the tune "Mean To Me" -- they did that one together, you know. It was really classic. He would play, and then he would back her when she sang. They did a beautiful trip, you know. And that was a fantastic night. Oh yeah, plenty of music was played that night. I'll always cherish those moments.
[INAUDIBLE COMMENT]

Oh yeah, before I get too far, I'd like to mention our trip to San Francisco. We had made one change in the band. J.D. King had left the band, and Tom Archia, a very fine tenor saxophonist, had joined us. For the trip to San Francisco we had... Bill Jones was still singing, with Tom Archia on tenor, Roy Porter on the drums, Bob Kesterson on bass, and Vernon Biddle playing the piano -- he was a very fine pianist.

And we played the Backstage in San Francisco. And it was a really nice place, with a high-rise stage. And again, Scatman Crothers was opposite of us, hah-hah, with his band. That's where I first met Bennie Green, the trombonist. He was in the Navy up there. And Jerome Richardson was in the Navy; I first met him...
T. Edwards - 152
You were in a band ...(?)...(?)...

Right. Up there at Treasure Island, I think it was. And the trombone player, Grover... Grover Mitchell, yeah. He was in the Navy. In fact, I think we were the first Bebop band they had ever heard! [LAUGHS]
And around San Francisco during that time, George Bledsoe was singing at a club called the California Club. That's where I first met him. And he's a great singer. He was playing piano and singing.
Doesn't he play bass?
Right, he plays bass. He plays saxophone, trumpet -- he plays several instruments. He's one of those very gifted guys that can do some of a lot of things. But he is a very fine singer.
[INAUDIBLE COMMENT]
Right. He was with one of the Ink Spots group, with the Stanley Morgan group, who was the guitar player with the original Howard McGhee band.
[INAUDIBLE COMMENT]

Yeah, I know. But he plays several instruments well. His strong thing was his singing, though. Really a great singer. In fact, later on, RCA-Victor recorded him, but didn't release the records, around 1948.
T. Edwards - 153
And, oh, I met Bernie Peters, the fantastic drummer from San Francisco. He was playing with George up there at the California Club. We used to go by there and sit in with them sometimes.
But anyway, the Backstage was really happening.
Where was it exactly?
It was on Powell just south of Geary -- on Powell Street. It was a big place.

And oh, it was really-really-really beautiful happenings then. We would go down to a place called... Oh, I can't think of the lady's name. Anyway, she had an after-hours place we used to go and eat, because she cooked these good hot biscuits. And Terry Gibbs was in the Army during that time. He had never heard anybody playing Bebop. He used to follow us around like a little kid. He'd pack his saxophone [sic?] around, whatever he needed to do at the time, just to be there to hear us place this music, you know. We could sit in with the horns down at the after-hour place, and he'd wait with his partner Beryl(?), who became his manager after he got his band later on...

We had a lot of nice times, all the guys would get up there and play. Because we were like the new thing, and the guys would hear you play and want to play with you. You know that routine, you know. Livin' fast...
T. Edwards - 154
What year?

This was February of '46. I'll never forget, my father wrote me a letter. He said, "Look, the war is winding down. Get out of California." He said, "Because it's no good for musicians and entertainers." He had been out here with shows years ago, you know, and he said "It's not the place to be." And sure enough, when we got back to San Francisco, the war was over, and the bottom had dropped out of Los Angeles! All the clubs had closed, you know, and it had just come to a standstill almost.

This is where I first met Al Hibbler. He was living at the Silver Thong(?). And the great Al Killian, the trumpet player, had been doing some work for Norman Granz on the Jazz At The Philharmonic, and decided to stay out here.

I'd like to mention a thing that happened with Al Killian. We all played an Army transcription with the band. The guy's name was Earl Spencer. You remember he used to do the Army transcriptions, make these transcriptions for the Army to play in different parts of the world? And I'll never forget, during the recording Al Killian was sitting on the far end of the bandstand, and the piano was on the other side. And during one of those arrangements, he played a double high C, and the double high C on the piano just screamed. I had never witnessed anything like that, you
T. Edwards - 155
know. When he played it, the piano just screamed, as if somebody, you know, struck the key. You know? [LAUGHS]
[INAUDIBLE COMMENT]
Oh yeah, he hit it right on the money. That's intonation, you know, when those sound waves are together. And that piano just screamed out.
This would be ...(?)...
Yeah. It was during the Army transcriptions.

Right, right. Service transcriptions. We also did one with Howard McGhee, with Danny Kaye, his first one, right after he had made his first movie. And another singer from England made her debut on that show, Miss Beryl Davis.
She later ended up ...(?)...
Oh, she did, huh? Well, she was quite a well-liked lady when she came over.
[PAUSE]

Most of the clubs on Central Avenue and the east side had folded, and things were beginning to move west music-wise. The next big music stop was Western Avenue. And it had places like the Ringside on Washington and Western. I used to play over there with Vi Redd's father, Alton Redd. He used to hire Wardell and me over there to play with them
T. Edwards - 156

quite often, and then just other guys would come in to jam. And the Hi-De-Ho Club. That's where Charlie Parker worked down with Wardell Gray, and Hampton, and Howard McGhee had the band. That's where they were when they recorded "Relaxin' At Camarillo," the recording...
That place was ...(?)...[INAUDIBLE]...(?)...
Might have been. Might have been. Yeah, that was at 50th and Western, a club called the Hi-De-Ho Club.
That's where Hamp was playing ...(?)...(?)..

No. I think... Wait a minute, now. Might have been! Because Hamp didn't get out of high school really until '46, I think. Sonny came out in '45. I think Hamp came out in '46. Might have been. I didn't play with that band, but I used to be in there all the time, you know.
And there was another place called Glenn's, just about 35th and Western, a place that used to serve barbecue...
Glenn's Barbecue.
Glenn's Barbecue, yeah. That's where I first met Carl Perkins, see.
He was playing ...(?)...(?)...
Yeah! The fantastic pianist, Carl Perkins, one of the real geniuses of the instrument. And in fact, he had his own way of playing his left hand. He sat sideways
T. Edwards - 157
to the piano, and his left arm was parallel to the keyboard. And he was quite a unique guy. And we worked together later on, which I will talk about. And what else was going on...
...(?)... they didn't advertise them.
No, they didn't advertise.
...(?)... music club and a barbecue restaurant. But Glenn and his wife liked music, and musicians liked his barbecue place, and there was a back room...

Right, it had a piano there. So they just started making the scene. It just happened, you know, on its own, more or less -- spontaneously. And a lot of great players used to come through there and make music.
Everybody(?).

Yeah. We all used to come down there and play. And during that time, the Oasis had started integrating the audience. And there was the Vinyl(?) Club on Western Avenue, you know, where they had floor shows and had the dancers and the... And good music.
38th and Western.

Right, 38th and Western. So Western Avenue became the scene, more or less. Later on, I worked at the Tiki there, at Mike's Tiki; that's when the first integrated that place, you know. Talk about integrated. Well, that's what was happening during those days, was integrating them!
T. Edwards - 158
Well, (?) Oasis was a White club.

Right, a White place. Same thing about Mike's. In fact, all those places on Western were White clubs. They didn't cater to just anybody that walked in. No. I remember the time you wouldn't dare walk in those places, you know. You'd be out of place!

But anyway, Western Avenue became a great street. A lot of great things happened up and down Western, and we used to eat at a place called the B&M. We used to get together there. Do you remember that one?
Right. South of Adams.
Yeah, right, just south of Adams. That's where I first met the guys with the... The Golden Gate Boys, remember them?
Mmm-hmm.
Yeah, they had the first big record on "Sold My Heart To the Jungle Man," with "Rain Water" and...
[PAUSE]

Yeah, times were pretty tough during this period. We used to take jobs and split them. Like, if I got a job, Wardell would go and play the job with me, and I'd split the money, and likewise, you know. One time, Wild Bill Moore had guys splitting gigs. He was like the impresario farming out the work, because he was still the good businessman, you
T. Edwards - 159

know... He would round up the work.
And we just kept going and kept going that way, until things started to coming around a little better, and they started having more concerts. During this period, I worked down at the Shriner Auditorium with Sarah Vaughan on the bill, and Art Tatum, and Erroll Garner (I had a little Jazz group on the bill) for Gene Norman Presents...yeah, at the Shriner...
Just Jazz.
Just Jazz, yeah. That was one of the biggies there. And I also did the thing at the Pasadena Civic for him, with Roy Eldridge and Charlie Ventura's band... Remember Charlie Ventura's band?
I was the press agent on those (?)s.
You were! [LAUGHS] The Trenier Twins were on the gig, yeah. And that was quite a night. I remember that one very well.
"Bop For The People."
"Bop For The People," yeah. It was pretty...
At that time you were (?) working at the Melody Club.
The Melody Club out on...
Slawson.
T. Edwards - 160
...Slawson, yeah, and broadcasting every night. Jimmy Witherspoon came in there with them later. Yeah, they were doing it over there.
[INAUDIBLE COMMENT]
Right-right-right!
Midnight from the Melody Club, and ...(?)... some melody.

[LAUGHS] Slim Gaillard was doing some work out at the Toddle(?) House out in Culver City, not only after that; he was out there at the Toddle(?) House and broadcasting from the kitchen, broadcasting recipes in different languages. [LAUGHS] Yeah, that was beautiful.

Yeah, we used to play the Sunday sessions at the Toddle House, Wardell and Sonny Criss and Hampton Hawes and Chuck Thompson and Roy Porter and all of us, and Kenny Bright, the trumpet, he would be on the scene with us. In fact, that's where I first met Warne Marsh. He was just coming on the scene. Him and Billy Byers, the trombone player, and fine arranger. They were just spreading their wings a little bit, you know. And Clifford Solomon, a very fine tenor saxophonist; he was just coming around by that time. And Hadley Caliman was on the scene, playing his tenor saxophone. He was really leaning heavily toward Dexter Gordon's thing, you know.
T. Edwards - 161
I don't remember Hadley Caliman from then.
Yeah, he was coming around during that period. Him and his little friend, Cecil; I can't remember Cecil's last name.
Anyway, I had a lot of nice things going on over there on Sundays and Tuesday evenings.

There was a person named Nancy Stovall who ...(?)... ...(?)... I remember a photograph taken in a photography magazine of Kenny Bright and I think Dexter Gordon, and I remember there was vapor coming out of Kenny Bright's horn.
No kidding?
...(?)... color picture. I recognized the bandstand ...(?)... [INAUDIBLE] ...(?)...
Manchester. Could that have been the Mayflower Ballroom?
It wasn't a ballroom.
It wasn't a ballroom?
No.
No, I don't remember any club until later on, when they had the Tropicana Club on Manchester.
Well, this was (?)49th or 50th(?)
49th or 50th. I don't remember a club on Manchester.
T. Edwards - 162
Later on? Joe Adams, the disk jockey, was involved in a club over there on Manchester called Arabian Nights. I worked over there with Sonny Criss, with a nice group over there.
Yeah, and then the people dressed in Arab-like costumes...heh-heh-heh... The waitresses, hah... Yeah, that was a nice engagement.
[PAUSE]

Right here, I'd like to mention some of the other people that I had the pleasure of working with that never made too much off a mark as far as people knowing them, but they were very excellent players. Like, Nathaniel Leeks, the trumpet player, who played with Gerald Wilson's band later and recorded with Gerald's band. Eric Dolphy was very ambitious at the time, and doing things.
And also a very fine alto player, Leroy Robertson. They called him Sweetpea. He worked with Roy Porter's band. But he had a very warm feeling and a beautiful sound on his instrument, you know.

And Hal Vernon, the pianist. In fact, Hal Vernon was one of the earlier...I hate to put it in this context...but earlier White piano players around Los Angeles who was really aware of the Bebop movement; you know, what they
T. Edwards - 163

called the Bebop movement. He was a very good writer, and played nice piano. Oh, and he was up on all of the tunes and everything. Later on, he wrote arrangements for Lionel Hampton's band. In fact, "Up In Dodo's Room" was his line, the one I recorded with Howard McGhee in 1945 I think it was... That was his line. And it's very, very modern for the time, you know. But he was a little bit nervous type guy, and a lot of people thought he was a little bit off. You know, they (?)called him off(?). But he was beautiful. But he loved music, you know, and...
He was around ...(? )...
Right, he used to be on the scene. Yeah, Harold Vernon. Very fine pianist. Fine writer.
Dodo was ...(? )...
Oh, Dodo Marmarosa. Yeah, well, he was around.
Barney Kessel was around during that time, playing. He hadn't been too long coming around here from Oklahoma.

And there was another fine tenor player named Johnny Beradino. He ended up being a card dealer in one of the hotels in Vegas. Hah-hah! But he was a very fine saxophone player. He had a great sound. Fine player.
We had some fine lady players coming along during that period, like Vi Redd, and Clora(?) Bryant, a trumpet player.
T. Edwards - 164
And Vivian Fears, a very fine pianist. Remember Vivian Fears? She played with the early Gerald Wilson Orchestra a few times. She was a very, very fine musician, a fine player.
And the Simon Brothers, Maurice and Freddie. Both of them played saxophones, and they did things... Freddie was a very fine songwriter also. And they were making marks during that period.

it was just about 1947 when I made my first recordings on my own. At the time he called the label MGM, and so MGM made him give up that title, and so then he named it Rem, and he changed it from Rem to Rex... But anyway, the things that I did...
Who was this man?
It was Murray Rappaport. Remember that name?
No.

Murray Rappaport owned a record store up on Hollywood Boulevard, just about a block east of Vine. And he would record people. He had recorded Art Tatum, Illinois Jacquet, several people. But this guy was a very shady character, ha-ha!, business-wise. He was about the best (?) I knew. He was the type of guy, if he could make more money doing a legitimate deal, he'd have to lose! Ha-ha...!
T. Edwards - 165
[END OF TAPE 4, SIDE B]

Anyway, I recorded with him. But I had a good contract! I had a good contract, and somehow... Somehow when it got to court, I was sold out. My attorney sold me out in court. In fact, the judge talked off the record about him for about 15 minutes. Because everybody knew he had a better case than what he was fighting, you know.
Q: [INAUDIBLE]

Well, I'm not going to mention his name. But anyway... And so, we had a postponement. And while we were waiting for the time to come around, Mr. Rappaport was jailed for selling pornographic magazines to kids. [LAUGHS] He ended up on Alcatraz.

Anyway, we did "Steady With Teddy" and "Bird Legs" and "Body And Soul" and "Roy's Boy," and Benny Bailey played a very beautiful solo all by himself on "Out Of Nowhere." All the compositions were mine, except "Out Of Nowhere" and "Body and Soul" and "Bird Legs," which was Benny Bailey's composition.

There was also a thing called "R.V.'s Wig." You remember R.V., who used to hang around the jam sessions, and he used to sell the records, like go from house to house selling records, and looking up rare records and hard-to-
T. Edwards - 166

find records for people. Anyway, he would be on the scene and he was a real music lover -- and he knew all of the solos on all of the records. All the latest records, he knew them. Like, at the jam sessions he'd be like the cheerleader, you know. [LAUGHS] He'd be pulling for his man, you know, leading the applause and everything. He was the kind of... I called it "R.V.'s Wig," because he had a fierce hairdo, a ...(?). and everything. And this was like in the middle Forties and in the early Fifties, through that period. He went to New York, but anyway, he saw him in 1964 in New York, and he was completely bald. I couldn't believe it! [LAUGHS] But he was a great guy and a music lover. He really worked hard for the musicians, you know. Like, these are the kind of people we need, you know, the people who help perpetuate the music.
Anyway, I did this date, and we got pretty good exposure. Honey Hancock was playing us on the radio station that he was on. Remember Honey Hancock?
[INAUDIBLE]
No, he wasn't on KGFJ. He was on another station up here, on Western Avenue and Third.
[INAUDIBLE]
Yeah. Might have been, yeah.
[INAUDIBLE]
T. Edwards - 167
Right. He went to KGFJ later. Yeah. And Joe Adams was playing these things, and...
No...
KOW.
KOW, yes, from Santa Monica. Yeah, he had his program out there. And we were getting really good action on these things. They were moving all around, you know.

And not too long after that, Dick Bock from Pacific Jazz and World Pacific Records, he did his first record date in the same little studio. He had a trumpet player named Louis Olsen(?) he brought from up north some place. And Wardell Gray and I worked the session with him. He had five saxophones and a trumpet and rhythm. And I wrote an arrangement for the group on one of my songs called "Before Dawn," for the five saxophones and the trumpet.
[INAUDIBLE]
Around about 1947. This was Dick Bock's first venture in recording.
This was before he was ...(?)...
Oh yeah. He hadn't been involved with records at all. This was his first venture into recording.
[INAUDIBLE]
T. Edwards - 168
Right. But he didn't even have a label at the time, I don't think. I don't remember. It didn't go far. It didn't go far. They pressed a few records, but it didn't go far.
[INAUDIBLE]
No, I don't remember the name of the label that they were pressed on.
Anyway, so, later on I did another date for the same fellow, Mister Rappaport. And this was Herbie Harper's first recording date, the trombonist. Yeah, we...
[INAUDIBLE]

We had Iggy Shaveck(?) and Hampton Hawes, and Roy Porter played the drums and I played the tenor. This was during the recording ban.. [LAUGHS] Yeah, but he paid us in cash money, so we went on and made that money [CHUCKLES] I think he wanted to kind of keep this over me, because I had this other good case against him, you know. He knew I had a very good case. But I hadn't gone to court at that time, you know.
But anyway...
What happened to these (?)?
They have been reissued on Onyx-Muse. All of these recordings, they have been reissued, and the things that I did on Dial Records were reissued on Onyx-Muse. It's
T. Edwards - 169

amazing how they located these recordings, because I didn't know anybody who knew where they were. And Rappaport, he was on Alcatraz; you know, he was in prison! I said, 'How could they find these records?' They never told me how they found these records, you know, after all of that time. They reissued them in about 1974 or '75; they reissued them then. [LAUGHS]
[INAUDIBLE]
Yeah. Bob Porter I think did the scouting for those things...

segments.title: Copyright notice and transcript header
segments.summary: Institute of Jazz Studies copyright warning and the title of the Teddy Edwards oral history.

segments.title: Birth in Jackson and his father the multi-instrumentalist
segments.summary: Edwards gives his birth date and place; his father played trombone and other instruments and read music superbly but left Jackson before he was born.

segments.title: Mother, siblings and grandparents
segments.summary: His epileptic mother stayed near her family, his father Bruce Marcus Edwards settled in Beaumont, and he was raised largely by his grandmother Malvina Smith Reed.

segments.title: Grandfather Fess Reed, early string bass player
segments.summary: His maternal grandfather Henry Carson Reed played upright bass in jazz bands around Mississippi, and Edwards later worked with him.

segments.title: The family steers him toward saxophone
segments.summary: Family pushed him toward his father's instrument, seating him by the saxophones at band rehearsals at home, amid church bands and medicine shows.

segments.title: Lessons with Arthur Horn and the first alto
segments.summary: A boarder, Arthur Horn, taught him for 35 cents a lesson paid in laundry; an uncle's C.G. Conn alto was acquired the same way.

segments.title: Winning the Alamo Theatre amateur contest and the Babe Ruth nickname
segments.summary: At 11 he won the Alamo Theatre talent contest three weeks running playing 'Jeep's Blues', and got the nickname Babe Ruth.

segments.title: Auditioning for Doc Palmer's band
segments.summary: Duke Holliston invites him to try out, they run parts on the porch, and he rehearses with a three-saxophone section at H.G. Hennington's house.

segments.title: Doc Palmer orchestra personnel
segments.summary: First rehearsal with the full band and a rundown of its trumpets, trombone, saxes and rhythm section, praising Doc Palmer's ears and power.

segments.title: Drummer Mark Hannah
segments.summary: Mark Hannah read drum parts and was among the first to use the hi-hat, far ahead of his time.

segments.title: Overlooked players: Banti and the Viper
segments.summary: He recalls a trombonist named Banti and a trumpeter called the Viper who played with the valve buttons removed.

segments.title: Touring at twelve and playing pig stands
segments.summary: Summer tours with Doc Palmer at twelve, then Sunday pig-stand gigs working for tips that Doc split.

segments.title: Bradley's nightclub across the Pearl River
segments.summary: Playing at Bradley's for fifty cents a night plus tips, learning to hear and make up tunes without written music.

segments.title: No child-labor worries, teaching himself clarinet
segments.summary: Tall for his age, he faced no objection; he saved for a clarinet and taught himself, since schools had one music teacher for eight Black schools.

segments.title: Learning chords and harmony on his own
segments.summary: After hearing of a visiting saxophonist who cut everyone running chords, he studies his father's harmony book and was writing orchestrations at fourteen.

segments.title: Don Dunbar's modern band
segments.summary: He joins Don Dunbar's more modern band with written arrangements, and lists its sidemen and sharp uniforms.

segments.title: Paul Gayten's Sizzling Six, Crystal Palace and WJDX broadcasts
segments.summary: He plays matinees with Paul Gayten's small group at the Crystal Palace and Savoy, broadcasts on WJDX, and hears visiting big bands.

segments.title: No recording in Jackson; Little Brother Montgomery and Mister Walters
segments.summary: Jackson had no recording equipment; local blues players like Little Brother Montgomery and Mister Walters went to Chicago to record.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: The Gay Floyd band from Little Rock
segments.summary: He praises an overlooked Arkansas band with a five-man reed section, a sleeper bus, writer Riley Hampton and entertainer Cleophus Jackson.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Segregated dances in Jackson
segments.summary: Ellington and Lunceford played only white dances in Jackson; at Black dances whites sat in roped-off seating.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Sneaking in to hear Johnny Hodges with Ellington
segments.summary: At fourteen he talks a doorman into letting him sit on the bandstand steps to hear his idol Johnny Hodges.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Bus tours and the Texas motorcycle patrolmen
segments.summary: Touring Alabama, Louisiana and Texas by bus; two patrolmen stopped the band and made them play for them.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Across the river in East Jackson
segments.summary: The all-night gambling and party district across the river, Stamps Brothers Hotel and Brother Reed's place where Paul Gayten made him sit on the piano.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: The Blue Flame and boogie-woogie player Bear Tracks
segments.summary: Joe Ketchum's Blue Flame club, and the barefoot boogie-woogie pianist Bear Tracks he later wrote a song about.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Shepherd's Cafe and pianist Coot Davis
segments.summary: Sitting in at Shepherd's Cafe with his grandfather on bass, soulful drummer Skinny Thomas and blues pianist Coot Davis.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Drummer Old Man Joe White and the Rotisserie
segments.summary: Old Man Joe White, parade drummer with the Rabbit Foot Minstrels, led street parades and demanded supper at every gig.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: The Silas Green show and Bessie Smith
segments.summary: The Silas Green From New Orleans tent show, which his father traveled with, had its own train cars and featured Bessie Smith.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Drummer Kid Lips Hackett and the minstrel-show bands
segments.summary: Kid Lips Hackett's stick tricks, later copied by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Payne, and Louis Jordan's start in the Rabbit Foot band.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: His father's embouchure lesson
segments.summary: His father tried to teach him double embouchure; he declined and went his own way.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: What a ballyhoo was
segments.summary: Explanation of ballyhooing: bands or shows playing on trucks or outside to draw a crowd.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Andy Kirk's band, Pha Terrell and Dick Wilson
segments.summary: He recalls Andy Kirk's organization, Mary Lou Williams, singer Pha Terrell and Dick Wilson's major-seventh sound in 1936.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Learning chord sounds and playing ad-lib by ear
segments.summary: He traces the minor seventh flat-five sound back to Mississippi and explains he learned chords rather than copying records.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Victrola and radio in the house
segments.summary: Cranked Victrola, Philco radio and the morning and afternoon broadcasts of the Mills Brothers, Ink Spots, Eddie South and Wayne King.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Hearing the bands on nationwide radio and at dances
segments.summary: Benny Goodman's Camel Caravan, Henderson and Hines from the Grand Terrace, territorial bands, and free admission to dances as a local musician.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Jukebox records and the Erskine Hawkins band
segments.summary: Ice cream parlor jukeboxes with Erskine Hawkins, Roy Eldridge and Krupa, and a rundown of Hawkins's sidemen.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: How devoted audiences were to the bands
segments.summary: People saved for weeks to dress for a dance, and many stood listening because radio and records were all there was; he compares Europe.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Lips Rose and the singer-director Edith Curry
segments.summary: Alto player Lips Rose in Louisiana and his wife Edith, an opera-trained singer who fronted and directed the band.

segments.chapter: Touring shows and the bands he heard
segments.title: Memphis, the Conway brothers and a Tennessee tour with Don Dunbar
segments.summary: The Conway brothers in Memphis, living near Beale Street, booking agent Dave Clark, and a Tennessee tour with a dancing, singing revue.

segments.title: School marks and skipping grades
segments.summary: A good memory made him a good student; one teacher blocked his skipping two grades, and the graduating class staged dances.

segments.title: Pressing clothes and learning instrument repair
segments.summary: He worked in the family cleaning business and learned repair from the one music-shop repairman who treated him as an equal.

segments.title: Piney Woods, Mississippi (poor audio)
segments.summary: Barely audible remarks about the Piney Woods school and another piano player.

segments.title: White gangs on the way to the stores
segments.summary: Segregation in Jackson: gangs of white boys ambushed Black children going to the chain stores across Capitol Street.

segments.title: Depression hardship and rationing
segments.summary: Checking garbage cans before school, stamps for goods, and his song 'Hard Times In '29'.

segments.title: Dealing with racism without hatred
segments.summary: A kind white storekeeper's family versus the places you had to avoid; he saw the hatred as taught sickness and chose to run before fighting.

segments.title: Louisiana police and dance rules across the South
segments.summary: Shreveport police clearing the streets after dances, a policeman blowing a whistle to end the dance, and mosquito smoke on bandstands.

segments.title: Chain-store helpers and delivering laundry
segments.summary: Unloading for store owners then being pelted with fruit, and gangs harassing children delivering white families' laundry.

segments.title: Police raid in Shreveport
segments.summary: Police burst into the Shreveport rooming house with the Dunbar orchestra and beat everyone with billy clubs; his thoughts on change in Jackson.

segments.title: Teaching Carl Lee Otis and his brother
segments.summary: He started a classmate, later a college band leader, on saxophone, and taught the brother clarinet by letters over notes.

segments.title: Jackson State, Cameron College and Jim Hill school
segments.summary: Names of Jackson's Black schools and colleges and the Reconstruction figures they were named for.

segments.title: Lanier High School band and contests
segments.summary: At Lanier High a real music program started; he helped teach and won band contests until disqualified as a professional.

segments.title: Leaving school for Detroit and the Bandbox
segments.summary: He leaves in the eleventh grade for his uncle's grocery in Detroit, and gets gigs at the Bandbox musicians' club where older players test him.

segments.title: Turf Bar and Jack Johnson's place
segments.summary: Sitting in at the Turf Bar and playing out on Eight Mile Road with pianist Johnny Van, who played to a dead sweetheart's pictures.

segments.title: Paradise Alley and meeting Yusef Lateef
segments.summary: The St. Antoine and Adams clubs where saxophonists jammed, and where he taught Yusef Lateef (then Bill Evans) his first chord changes.

segments.title: Hastings Street and the Ace Bar
segments.summary: Hastings Street's games, bars and pimps, his first job there with George E. Lee, and Milt Jackson jamming around.

segments.title: Meeting Gene Ammons at the Champion Bar
segments.summary: At the Champion Bar he first met Gene Ammons with King Kolax's band, and heard a bluesy tenor named Effie.

segments.title: Pimps' Cadillac funerals and nightclub owners
segments.summary: Cadillac funerals for pimps and club owners who bought rounds in each other's bars.

segments.title: T-Bone Walker at the Three Sixes
segments.summary: First seeing T-Bone Walker at the Three Sixes and crediting him with opening up guitar playing.

segments.title: The Treniers' band and Sonny Stitt
segments.summary: The Trenier Twins' big band came through Detroit with Sonny Stitt, Joe Morris, Don Hill and Morris Lane.

segments.title: Lucky Thompson, Willie Anderson and the young altos
segments.summary: Meeting Lucky Thompson and the pack of young Detroit altos, with his grandmother pulling him back and forth to Jackson.

segments.title: Pearl Harbor night at Enrico's
segments.summary: On the night of Pearl Harbor he was playing a female-impersonator floor show at Enrico's, and he also did taxi dances.

segments.title: Joining the musicians' union
segments.summary: He joined the Detroit union in 1941, which had one Black representative, and heard many local trumpeters.

segments.title: Hank Jones trio, his uncle's family and Tweed Beard
segments.summary: Working on Grand River with Johnny Johnson and Hank Jones, the kindness of his Detroit relatives, and starting with bassist Tweed Beard.

segments.title: Tenor saxophonist Eddie Loven
segments.summary: He praises Eddie Loven, a warm-toned Detroit tenor who died at 24 without recording, and Julius Watkins.

segments.title: Detroit's school music system and Cass Tech
segments.summary: Cass Tech's training counted as junior college; he passed its aptitude test but explains later why he left.

segments.title: Joe Louis, Sugar Ray and the numbers racket
segments.summary: Neighborhood memories of Joe Louis at Brewster Center, Sugar Ray, and Detroit's gambling and numbers culture.

segments.title: WPA bands and Little Sam's
segments.summary: The government-sponsored WPA bands he heard rehearse, and gigs at Little Sam's in Black Bottom.

segments.title: White saxophonists he admired
segments.summary: Johnny Bothwell, Hal McIntyre, Dave Matthews and Sam Donohue as players who broke from the heavy-vibrato mold.

segments.title: Big bands at the Michigan and Paradise theatres
segments.summary: Seeing Sinatra with Dorsey and the Black bands, including Basie, Hines with Eckstine and Sarah Vaughan, at the Paradise.

segments.title: Tap dancers and acts at the Paradise Theatre
segments.summary: Butterbeans and Susie, Honi Coles, Baby Lawrence, Bunny Briggs and Bill Robinson on the Paradise bill.

segments.title: Graystone Ballroom: Hampton, Hines and Coleman Hawkins
segments.summary: The Graystone Ballroom bands, Hampton's first band, outings with Aunt Lydia to hear Earl Hines, and Hawkins's 'Body and Soul'.

segments.title: Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan and Lil Green
segments.summary: First hearing Billie Holiday and Sarah Vaughan at the Paradise and loving Lil Green, whom Peggy Lee later credited.

segments.title: Tweed Beard and the Glenn Miller era
segments.summary: Working with bassist Tweed Beard around the time Glenn Miller was hot.

segments.title: Fats Waller and Trombone Smitty at the Paradise
segments.summary: Fats Waller's local band drank 52 fifths in a week, and Trombone Smitty brought the house down with one eight-bar bridge.

segments.title: George Nicholson and the Benny Carter influence
segments.summary: A new tenor player in Tweed Beard's band, and how young altos like Stitt and Wardell Gray modeled themselves on Benny Carter.

segments.title: The Congo Club and Big Nick
segments.summary: The Congo Club in the Norwood Hotel, where he joined the house band and Big Nick encouraged him.

segments.title: Learning diaphragm breathing
segments.summary: A bandmate teaches him diaphragm breathing; he practices constantly and within six months is leading the section.

segments.title: Congo Club band personnel
segments.summary: Personnel of the Congo Club band, with Maurice King writing and later Matthew Gee, Wardell Gray and Ted Buckner joining.

segments.title: Giving up Cass Tech to stay with the band
segments.summary: With the show rehearsals it was too hard to keep both, so he left school in the eleventh grade despite his principal's letter.

segments.title: The band as a family
segments.summary: Late breakfasts, late movies and visits from musicians like Bob Mitchell; he calls it a highlight of his career.

segments.title: The clarinet falls apart during his solo
segments.summary: During a featured clarinet solo the cracked lower half of the horn dropped on the floor.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: The club closes and the band breaks up
segments.summary: The owner Mister Jones died and his niece closed the club; his grandmother fell ill and died.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Drafted and rejected
segments.summary: After a party at Al McKibbon's he is examined for the draft and rejected because of his broken arm; also luck at dice.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Leading a band in Alexandria, Louisiana
segments.summary: After the funeral he joins a group playing Alexandria near Camp Polk, is voted leader, and meets Lips Rose again.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Wat Sanders' Blue Room in Tampa and pianist Chick Stephens
segments.summary: The band takes a Tampa job where he meets Art Tatum-class pianist Chick Stephens.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Baby Lockett, Jack Scott and the young Cannonball Adderley
segments.summary: Band changes and the St. Petersburg kids, including Cannonball and Nat Adderley, who listened outside.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Hearing the new Billy Eckstine band in Florida
segments.summary: He hears Eckstine's band days after forming, with Parker, Dizzy, Blakey, Sarah and Lucky Thompson.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Meeting Charlie Parker in Detroit and Lakeland
segments.summary: He first met Parker in Detroit with McShann, Ben Webster raved about his 'Cherokee', and Parker had memorized the Eckstine book.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Ernie Fields recruits him
segments.summary: Wild Bill Moore appears in Tampa, and Ernie Fields's men hear him and persuade the leader to hire him.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: His father's visit and the trip west
segments.summary: His father, still with Silas Green, advised going to New York; Fields's route kept leading him farther away.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Ernie Fields band personnel
segments.summary: Singer Melvin Moore, the reed section, pianist Lee Wesley Jones, the ear-learning trombonist Tain and others.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Tricked into the territory route; Baltimore Royal Theatre
segments.summary: Fields took the band to Nebraska instead of New York, then followed Benny Carter and Nat Cole at Baltimore's Royal.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Tulsa layoff, the Barn and Max Roach's Stravinsky
segments.summary: Layoff in Tulsa where he met Max Roach and J.J. Johnson, jammed at the Barn with Harry Pettiford, and first heard Stravinsky.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Arriving at Club Alabam and the Downbeat on Central Avenue
segments.summary: First night on Central Avenue and the layout of the Downbeat, his all-time favorite club.

segments.chapter: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
segments.title: Sid Catlett at the Downbeat
segments.summary: On a break he hears Sid Catlett with Allan Eager's quartet.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: After-hours places along San Pedro
segments.summary: Casablanca, Cafe Society, Big Jim Wynn, and other late places on San Pedro, with Red Mack and Tom Archia.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Shepp's Playhouse and Eddie Heywood
segments.summary: Gerald Wilson's band upstairs and combos below at Shepp's, and Eddie Heywood's group's hit.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Northwest and Canadian tour with Fields
segments.summary: Club Alabam ended, then Portland, Seattle and Victoria, where Canadian audiences knew his name.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Roy Milton's standing offer and the union
segments.summary: He sat in with Roy Milton's group at the Cobra Room, and Milton promised a job and union membership.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Bus breakdown near Cheyenne and leaving Fields
segments.summary: The bus broke down in a freezing Wyoming winter, so he left Fields and called Roy Milton to return to California.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Back with Roy Milton and young Sonny Criss, Big Jay McNeely
segments.summary: Back at the Cobra Room, and living at the Civic Hotel as teenagers Sonny Criss and Big Jay McNeely listened from the doorway.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: The Civic Hotel residents and comedian Willie Lewis
segments.summary: Gene Montgomery and comedian Willie Lewis lived at the Civic Hotel, the funniest man he knew and a baton twirler.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Roy Milton's band and tenor Buddy Floyd
segments.summary: Camille Howard, Roy's entertaining blues band, and Buddy Floyd's economy of notes that influenced his own slow blues.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Gerald Wilson's band and Central Avenue after-hours
segments.summary: Gerald Wilson's band with Melba Liston at Shepp's and the after-hours places on Central.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Joe Morris' Plantation and the Eckstine band again
segments.summary: The Plantation at 97th and Central, and the Eckstine band's new personnel; Dizzy rehearsing 'Woody 'n You'.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Billy Berg's club and Slim Gaillard
segments.summary: Billy Berg's club, the Truville, Slim Gaillard's group, and nightly broadcasts with no cover.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Sunday sessions with Hampton Hawes and Wardell Gray
segments.summary: Sunday jam sessions with Hawes, Sonny Criss, Wardell Gray and other session regulars.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
segments.title: Hollywood clubs: Radio Room, Hangover and the Empire Room
segments.summary: Lucky Thompson at the Radio Room, Dixieland at the Hangover, and Woody Herman's Four Brothers.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Howard McGhee asks him to switch to tenor
segments.summary: McGhee stays in LA after Billy Berg's and asks him to learn tenor; in six weeks he could hear it.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Forming McGhee's group and the Downbeat opening
segments.summary: The first McGhee band personnel, their modern ambition as West Coast counterparts of Parker and Gillespie, and the union.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Roy Porter and the cymbal stand
segments.summary: Roy Porter replaces the older drummer and turns Edwards's music stand into a cymbal stand.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Swing Club job opposite Scatman Crothers
segments.summary: The McGhee band in new uniforms alternates with Scatman Crothers's band at the Swing Club.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Parker and Gillespie at Billy Berg's; the Casablanca
segments.summary: Gillespie and Parker's band at Berg's, hanging out at the Casablanca, and Frank Morgan's arrival.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Parker's 'Lover Man' night and the Casablanca crowd
segments.summary: A night when Parker's 'Lover Man' chorus left no one willing to play, plus local singers and Kenny Bright.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Jack's Basket Room and Wild Bill Moore as impresario
segments.summary: After-hours at Jack's Basket Room where Wild Bill Moore handled the hiring.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Ross Russell, Dial Records and 'Moose The Mooche'
segments.summary: Ross Russell's Tempo store leads to Parker's first Dial date; Parker sings 'Moose The Mooche' for Moose the paraplegic fan.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: 'Up In Dodo's Room' and his influence on Coltrane's generation
segments.summary: His McGhee recording for Tempo; Fats Navarro said the solo broke from the Young and Hawkins schools, and Coltrane and others studied it.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: First professional recording for the Bihari brothers
segments.summary: The Modern Records session with McGhee, 'Deep Meditation', in which he echoed Coleman Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Tenor solo on 'They Shoot Horses, Don't They?'
segments.summary: For the film's 1932 setting he played with Chu Berry in mind, and Shelly Manne guessed it; personnel of the soundtrack.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Rumor of a secretly recorded McGhee band
segments.summary: A story that the band was secretly recorded through a ceiling microphone, which he does not know about.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Backing Wynonie Harris on 'Around The Clock'
segments.summary: The McGhee band backed Wynonie Harris on his first hit, with a solo by Edwards.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Other labels and the honking show-business routine
segments.summary: Philo, the Messner brothers' label, and the honking tenor battle with J.D. King that Howard McGhee staged.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Players back East studying him; fast tenor and Chico Hamilton
segments.summary: Coltrane and others checked him out, he was among the first to play fast tenor, and Chico Hamilton remembered him.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: The Lincoln Theatre, Billy Eckstine and Cecil Gant
segments.summary: McGhee's big band at the Lincoln, and the crowd booing the Eckstine band because they wanted Private Cecil Gant.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: How big the Lincoln was; Bill Robinson and Orpheum theatres
segments.summary: The Lincoln as less consistent than the Apollo, the Bill Robinson Theatre and shows at the Orpheum.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Will Roland and Charlie Parker's courtesy
segments.summary: Showman Will Roland, who couldn't play, pushed Parker aside at the Jungle Room; Parker listened politely, since 'everybody's got something'.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Illinois Jacquet and Calvin Jackson at the Swing Club
segments.summary: Meeting Illinois Jacquet, who tried to recruit him, and pianist Calvin Jackson sitting in.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Streets of Paris, Kay Starr and Erroll Garner
segments.summary: Working the Streets of Paris basement, with the Four Blazers and Kay Starr, and Garner across the street.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: The Jade Room opposite Kid Ory
segments.summary: A modern band alternating with Kid Ory's Dixielanders at the Jade Room, owned by 'Mother Goddamn'.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Movie stars and rising musicians on the scene
segments.summary: Film stars like Sonny Tufts, Ava Gardner and Orson Welles came to the clubs, along with young musicians who became famous.

segments.chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
segments.title: Pianist Duke Brooks and bassist Iggy Shavack
segments.summary: Remembering pianist Duke Brooks and bassist Iggy Shavack.

segments.title: Living with Charlie Parker on Vernon Avenue
segments.summary: Parker moves in with him and Gene Montgomery in late 1945; Miles Davis and Stan Getz appear on the scene.

segments.title: Musicians move west; nights at Jack's Basket Room
segments.summary: The war brought musicians west, Leonard Feather arrived, and he lists the all-star nights at Jack's Basket Room.

segments.title: Playing with Art Tatum at the St. Francis
segments.summary: Tatum hired Edwards and others for a gig and played with childlike enthusiasm.

segments.title: Tijuana trip with Parker
segments.summary: Parker went to Tijuana and wouldn't come back to work, while Dizzy stayed to handle business.

segments.title: Sammy Yates and the Dial dates
segments.summary: Sammy Yates persuaded Parker to record 'Just Friends'; Edwards recalls the first Dial session personnel.

segments.title: Parker's greatest blues at a San Pedro dive
segments.summary: At a Saturday jam in a blues joint, Parker sat on a 4-by-4 seat and played the greatest blues Edwards heard from him.

segments.title: Howard McGhee's Finale Club band
segments.summary: McGhee's house where the Treniers lived, and the Finale Club band with Parker, Criss, Montgomery and Edwards during the recording ban.

segments.title: Parker's breakdown begins; 'The Gypsy' and 'Idaho'
segments.summary: Parker's nerves collapsed at the Finale Club, yet he played unforgettable moments on 'The Gypsy' and 'Idaho'.

segments.title: Parker taken to hospital and the beach outings from Camarillo
segments.summary: Parker was strapped down in the General Hospital and sent to Camarillo; friends took him out to play on the beach.

segments.title: Parker's drug use and practice habits
segments.summary: Parker told him he began hard drugs at fourteen, out-practiced everyone, and visited Buster Smith in Dallas.

segments.title: Parker's release from Camarillo and the big night at Jack's Basket
segments.summary: Parker is moved into Leroy's house and plays a star-filled set with June Christy including 'Mean To Me'.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: Trip to San Francisco and the Backstage
segments.summary: Band change with Tom Archia, a Backstage engagement opposite Scatman Crothers, and Navy players Bennie Green, Jerome Richardson and Grover Mitchell.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: George Bledsoe at the California Club
segments.summary: Singer-multi-instrumentalist George Bledsoe, whom RCA recorded in about 1948, and Bernie Peters.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: The Backstage and Terry Gibbs
segments.summary: The Backstage on Powell Street, an after-hours cook, and soldier Terry Gibbs following the bebop players around.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: Postwar collapse of Los Angeles
segments.summary: His father's letter warned him to leave California; back in LA the clubs had closed, and he met Al Hibbler and Al Killian.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: Army transcriptions with Al Killian
segments.summary: Earl Spencer's Army transcriptions where Killian's high C made the piano scream, and a Danny Kaye show with McGhee.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: Western Avenue: the Ringside and Hi-De-Ho Club
segments.summary: With Central Avenue clubs closing, Western Avenue took over, including Alton Redd's Ringside and the Hi-De-Ho Club.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: Glenn's Barbecue and Carl Perkins
segments.summary: Glenn's Barbecue's back-room sessions where he first met pianist Carl Perkins.

segments.chapter: San Francisco and the postwar slump
segments.title: Integrating the Western Avenue clubs, B&M
segments.summary: White clubs like the Oasis began to integrate, and he mentions the B&M and the Golden Gate Boys.

segments.title: Hard times, split gigs and Gene Norman concerts
segments.summary: Musicians split jobs, and he played Gene Norman's Just Jazz concerts and the Melody Club broadcasts.

segments.title: Toddle House and Sunday sessions
segments.summary: Slim Gaillard at the Toddle House, and Sunday sessions where he met Warne Marsh, Clifford Solomon and Hadley Caliman.

segments.title: Locating a Kenny Bright photograph; Arabian Nights
segments.summary: A discussion of where a Dexter Gordon photo was taken, and working at Arabian Nights on Manchester with Sonny Criss.

segments.title: Overlooked Los Angeles players
segments.summary: A list of underrecognized players including Hal Vernon, Barney Kessel, Vi Redd, Vivian Fears and the Simon brothers.

segments.title: Murray Rappaport's label and the lawsuit
segments.summary: His first recordings on Murray Rappaport's label, a shady dealing and a lost court case; Rappaport later jailed.

segments.title: Rappaport session titles and R.V.'s Wig
segments.summary: Titles from the session, and the record-selling fan R.V. who inspired 'R.V.'s Wig'.

segments.title: Radio airplay by Honey Hancock and Joe Adams
segments.summary: The records got radio play on Honey Hancock's and Joe Adams's shows.

segments.title: Dick Bock's first recording session
segments.summary: Dick Bock's first date with a trumpeter and five saxophones including Wardell Gray, featuring Edwards's 'Before Dawn'.

segments.title: Herbie Harper date and the later reissues
segments.summary: Another Rappaport date with Hampton Hawes and Roy Porter, later reissued on Onyx-Muse.
